title: Living ashtpadi 8
hook: the brahm giaanee is a portrait to grow into, not a title to claim

segments.voice: Yesterday, like the earth: dug by one, anointed by another, the same to both. Your line was like the earth. Today, we live ashtpadi eight. Day four hundred sixty-nine, the end of a week.

A child puts on her father's shoes and clomps around the kitchen. They're enormous. She trips. Everyone laughs, and nobody thinks she's pretending to be him. She's trying them on. She's leaning toward a size she'll grow into one day. There's a world of difference between that child and someone who buys a uniform and starts giving orders. One is growing. The other is claiming. Ashtpadi eight's portrait of the brahm giaanee can be worn either way. Sikh teachers have long warned which way not to wear it.
screen: `A CHILD IN HER FATHER'S SHOES.` → `TRYING ON, NOT PRETENDING.` → `GROWING, OR CLAIMING?`

segments.voice: Ashtpadi eight paints its portrait for eight stanzas. True in mind and mouth. A lotus in water. The sun, the wind, the earth, the fire. And more: the God-conscious one is filled with humility, gareebee, the word that also means being poor, low, unassuming. The God-conscious one delights in doing good for others. Friend and enemy look the same to them. And then, deep in the ashtpadi, a line that stops the whole thing becoming a checklist: only a brahm giaanee knows the state of a brahm giaanee. In other words, you can't assess it from outside, and you certainly can't award it to yourself. Put the humility and that line together, and a quiet logic appears. Anyone who announces I am a brahm giaanee has just shown a lack of the very first quality in the portrait. That's why Sikh teachers often say: read ashtpadi eight as a mirror and a direction, never as a label. Living it means picking one quality, the earth's patience, the lotus's dryness, the wind's fairness, and growing into it, a little, the way a child grows into shoes. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, the holy company: the face growing bright, ego leaving quietly, and company chosen like food. Then the brahm giaanee: true inside and out, a lotus, and the earth. A week of good people. One portrait to grow toward.
screen: `GAREEBEE: HUMILITY, LOWLINESS.` · `ONLY THEY KNOW THAT STATE.` · `TO CLAIM IT IS TO LACK IT.` · `ONE QUALITY, A LITTLE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `GROW INTO IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: practice one quality from the portrait. Pick one. The lotus: in the mess, untouched. The earth: the same to the one who digs and the one who honors. The wind: fair to king and beggar. Gareebee: humble, low, unassuming. Don't pick the hardest. Pick the one that feels like a shoe slightly too big. Hold it in mind. Breathe in its name. Breathe out, and picture one moment today where you could try it on. If you pray, you can ask for help to grow. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi eight. The brahm giaanee is a portrait to grow into, with humility at its heart, never a title to claim.
Your line: grow into it. Today, try on your one quality once, and tell no one you're doing it. Day four hundred sixty-nine. A week, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs read ashtpadi eight of Sukhmani Sahib as a portrait of qualities to cultivate, and many teachers caution against anyone claiming the title brahm giaanee for themselves.

pairs: the same to digger and anointer

it says only a brahm giaanee knows that state; it can't be assessed or claimed.

gareebee, and eagerness to do good.

fork.setup: you've read ashtpadi eight and recognize yourself in one line. what now?
options: tell your friends you're nearly a brahm giaanee.
pick one quality and quietly grow into it.
decide it's too high and give up.
fork.reveal: the portrait is a direction, not a label: grow into it, a little at a time.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gareebee, humility, lowliness; in ashtpadi eight, the brahm giaanee is filled with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: brahm giaanee is a rank some people reach.
what it means: it's a portrait to grow toward, with humility at its center.
what a scholar hears: 'brahm giaanee kee gat brahm giaanee jaanai' makes the state self-attesting only; Sikh writers have long cautioned against its use as a self-claimed title.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
